title: Traversing with Pointers
concept: You can scan the array by moving the pointer (p) instead of the index (i).

steps.title: with header
steps.explanation:
Use the output function with `#include <stdio.h>`.

This lesson covers patterns for traversing an array using pointer movement (`p++`) without an index.

steps.title: Start main function
steps.explanation:
After creating the main frame, prepare the array and pointer.

Afterwards, `p` is moved one space at a time and the value is read.

steps.title: array declaration
steps.explanation:
The `-1` at the end of `arr` is a sentinel value that signals the end of the traversal.

Using Sentinel, you can determine the end without having to set a separate length variable.

steps.title: pointer initialization
steps.explanation:
`p = arr` makes `p` point to the first element.

Now you can read `*p` in a loop and move to the next element with `p++`.

steps.title: while (*p != -1)
steps.explanation:
The condition checks whether the current value is a sentinel (`-1`).

Repeat until you encounter a Sentinel, at which point you immediately end your traversal.

steps.title: p++ (Pointer Increment)
steps.explanation:
`p++` moves to the next element, the amount of movement is `sizeof(int)`.

Pointers can be incremented, but array names cannot be incremented.

steps.title: Output value by dereference
steps.explanation:
Printing `*p` in each iteration will output 10, 20, and 30 in that order.

The key is to keep the three elements of "read(`*p`) + move(`p++`) + termination condition" stable.

steps.title: Condition check: *p is 20 (not -1)
steps.explanation:
`*p` is now `20`, so the loop continues.

Each iteration: check condition -> print -> advance pointer.

steps.title: Iteration 2: Print *p (20)
steps.explanation: Prints the value at `0x1004`, which is `20`.

steps.title: Iteration 2: p++ moves to next element
steps.explanation:
`p++` advances from `0x1004` to `0x1008`.

Now `p` points to `arr[2]` which holds `30`.

steps.title: Condition check: *p is 30 (not -1)
steps.explanation: `*p` is `30`, so the loop continues for one more iteration.

steps.title: Iteration 3: Print *p (30)
steps.explanation: Prints the value at `0x1008`, which is `30`. This is the last valid element.

steps.title: Iteration 3: p++ moves past last element
steps.explanation:
`p++` advances from `0x1008` to `0x100c`.

Now `p` points to `arr[3]` which holds the sentinel value `-1`.

steps.title: Loop exits: *p is -1 (sentinel found)
steps.explanation:
`*p` is now `-1`, so `*p != -1` is false and the loop terminates.

The sentinel value successfully stopped the traversal at the right point.

steps.title: Program exit
steps.explanation:
`return 0;` terminates the program.

The key pattern: read (`*p`) + move (`p++`) + sentinel termination condition.

quiz.question: What should I pay attention to when iterating an array with pointer p?
options: There is a risk of going out of bounds.
p++ only moves 1 byte at a time
quiz.explanation:
The pointer has no brakes.
If the termination condition (`length` reached or `NULL` character) is set incorrectly, reading continues beyond the end of the array and a memory error occurs.

misconceptions.wrong: These days, compilers are much faster for pointers (p++) than for indexes (arr[i]).
misconceptions.correct: It was like that in the past, but now it's similar because compiler optimization is good.
misconceptions.why:
For readability, it is often better to use an index (`arr[i]`).
There is no need to force yourself to use pointers.

keyTakeaway: Scanning an array with `p++` is a dream of the C language. But beware of cliffs (exceeding the range).
